strengths: Introduces Visual Information Gain (VIG), a simple, model-agnostic metric that quantifies visual contribution at both sample and token levels with a clear decomposition into per-token loss differences.

Demonstrates strong data efficiency: training with VIG-guided selection reduces active tokens by up to 79% (e.g., LLaVA-1.5 13B) while improving or maintaining performance across multiple vision understanding and hallucination benchmarks.
Shows complementarity with existing training-free (VCD, PAI, VAR) and training-based (LACING) methods, yielding additive gains when combined.
Provides supporting analyses: increased attention to visual tokens and improved robustness to textual corruption, which are consistent with the claimed reduction in language bias.
Extensive experiments across three models (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, ShareGPT4V 7B) and seven benchmarks, with ablation studies on selection level and ratio.
weaknesses: Inconsistent numbers across tables: Table 5 (main text) reports SS+TS CHAIR C_S = 49.10 and MMHal Hall. = 61.82, while Table E.1 reports 47.00 and 62.78 for the same configuration; LLaVAW also differs (61.19 vs 61.22). This raises reproducibility concerns.

Table 4 caption states that values in parentheses indicate improvement over the vanilla model, but for combined methods (e.g., VIG training + VCD) the numbers actually indicate improvement over the corresponding single method, which is confusing and potentially misleading.
Missing a key baseline: random token selection with the same token retention rate, which is needed to isolate the benefit of VIG-based token selection from mere token reduction.

The token-level threshold is set equal to the sample-level threshold τ_p, an arbitrary choice that leads to very different token retention rates across models (e.g., 75% vs 42%) and is not justified beyond avoiding an extra hyperparameter.

The theoretical analysis (Eqs. 3–5) is essentially a restatement of the cross-entropy difference and provides little deep insight; the KL divergence formulation becomes tautological under deterministic (one-hot) supervision.
Performance gains over existing methods are modest, and VIG training alone underperforms LACING on MMVet and MMBench.
The attention analysis is correlational and does not establish causality, and the 'blind faith in text' corruption protocol is only briefly described.
No comparison to other data selection criteria (e.g., loss-based, diversity-based) to demonstrate that VIG is superior to alternative heuristics.

strengths: Introduces a simple and intuitive metric (VIG) based on perplexity difference that is easy to compute and interpret for both samples and tokens.
Demonstrates data efficiency: reduces sample tokens by 13-51% and active tokens by 34-79% while improving performance on several vision understanding and hallucination benchmarks.
Shows orthogonality with existing methods (VCD, PAI, VAR, LACING), with additive gains when combined.
Provides insightful analyses, including increased attention to visual tokens and reduced language bias under textual corruption.
Includes ablation studies on selection ratio p and selection levels, offering practical guidance.
Acknowledges computational overhead and limited architecture generalization in the limitations section.
Provides detailed hyperparameters, thresholds, and training configurations for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Missing a critical baseline: random token selection within the selected samples. Without this, the improvement from token-level VIG selection cannot be attributed to VIG itself rather than simply reducing the number of tokens.

The token-level selection threshold tau_p can be negative (e.g., -0.021 for LLaVA-1.5 7B), meaning tokens with negative VIG are included, contradicting the stated goal of focusing on visually informative tokens.

The use of a blurred image to simulate visual absence is a heuristic that is not validated; blur parameters are unspecified, and it is unclear whether the blurred image truly removes all visual information.
Many reported improvements are marginal and lack statistical significance testing (e.g., POPE F1 +0.03, DocVQA +0.20); no error bars or multiple seeds are provided.

High computational overhead: VIG computation takes ~6 hours on 8 RTX 4090 GPUs, plus ~7 hours of training, roughly doubling total compute compared to vanilla training, which offsets the claimed data efficiency.
No comparison against other data selection methods (e.g., loss-based, entropy-based, or active learning baselines); only random sample selection is used as a baseline.
The theoretical justification (Eq. 4 to Eq. 5) is trivial under one-hot targets and does not provide meaningful insight beyond the definition.
Limited evaluation to LLaVA-1.5 and ShareGPT4V, both sharing the same architecture, so generalization to other LVLM families is unproven.
Potential data selection bias is not discussed; selecting high-VIG samples may over-represent certain visual concepts and harm model diversity.
Related work is thin and does not engage with the broader data selection or active learning literature for multimodal models.
Token-level VIG validation is only qualitative (example tokens in Table 2); no systematic quantitative evaluation against human annotations or object detectors is provided.

strengths: Clean, well-motivated, and theoretically grounded metric. The derivation of VIG as a cross-entropy/KL decomposition (Eqs. 3–5) and its token-level decomposition (Eq. 6) give the measure an interpretable foundation rather than being an ad hoc heuristic.

Strong empirical validation of the metric itself. The MS-COCO sensitivity example (Tab. 1) and the benchmark-level distribution analysis (Fig. 2) show VIG behaves as expected (positive for aligned images, negative for conflicting ones; COCO/POPE more visual, GQA/SQA more text-dominant), and the token-level scatter (Fig. 3, Tab. 2) recover interpretable, visually grounded tokens (colors, spatial relations, states) versus syntactic tokens.

Practical, demonstrated utility across three models and seven benchmarks. VIG-guided selective training reduces supervision by 13–79% while matching or improving vision understanding and hallucination metrics, with particularly striking results for LLaVA-1.5 13B (12.14M active tokens, all benchmarks improved).

Good ablation structure: random-vs-VIG sample selection (SS) isolates the effect of VIG-based filtering, and SS+TS shows the value of token-level selection; the selection-ratio study (Fig. 6, Tab. E.3) is reported honestly even where it is unflattering.
Demonstrated orthogonality to existing approaches (VCD, PAI, VAR, LACING), with additive gains when combined, which strengthens the claim that VIG is a complementary data-centric signal.

Mechanistic evidence supporting the mechanism: increased attention to visual tokens (Fig. 4, Fig. D.1) and improved robustness to corrupted text (Fig. 5, Fig. D.2) are consistent with the stated hypothesis about reduced language bias.

Reproducibility is reasonably good: thresholds τ_p (Tab. C.1, E.2), training hyperparameters (Tab. C.2), and implementation details are provided, and the method requires no architectural change or inference overhead.
weaknesses: No variance or error bars are reported anywhere, yet many headline gains are small (e.g., DocVQA +0.20, POPE F1 +0.03, MMBench +0.87). Without multiple seeds or significance testing, it is hard to distinguish real improvements from run-to-run noise, which is decisive for the data-efficiency claims.

The selection ratio ablation reveals a worrying instability on MMBench: p=30 and p=50 yield 56.87 and 56.44 versus the 65.46 baseline (Tab. E.3), i.e., VIG selection can degrade performance by ~9 points on broad-coverage reasoning, with only a narrow sweet spot at p=70. Similarly, sample-level selection alone (SS) drops MMBench to 57.56, then SS+TS jumps to 66.33 (Tab. 5, Tab. E.1). These large, unexplained discontinuities raise questions about the robustness and generality of the selection criterion and are not adequately analyzed.

For a paper whose central claim is about data selection, there is no comparison to standard data-pruning / importance-selection baselines (e.g., loss-based, EL2N, coreset, or even tuned random selection at matched budgets). The only data-centric baseline is a single untuned random 70% subset, which is a weak control for a data-selection contribution.

The 'visual absence' simulation uses a Gaussian blur (Appendix B), inherited from prior work, but the blur parameters are not specified and no sensitivity analysis is given. Since the entire VIG computation rests on this proxy, its fidelity matters, and blurring leaves residual low-frequency cues that could bias the text-only PPL estimate.

The 'model-agnostic' claim is overstated: VIG is computed with a specific aligned (pre-training-stage) checkpoint, so scores are model- and alignment-dependent (the paper itself notes thresholds and retained-token fractions differ across models), which limits reuse across architectures as claimed.

The theoretical framing is somewhat loose. The statement that incorporating I 'in general reduces the intrinsic uncertainty' (justifying Eq. 5) is asserted rather than established, and the deterministic-supervision simplification collapses much of the analysis, so the formal connection between Eq. 4 and the empirically measured quantity is weaker than presented.

The causal framing that language bias is 'driven by the prevalence of weakly grounded, text-dominant examples' is a hypothesis that is not directly tested (e.g., no controlled experiment varying the proportion of low-VIG data), so the attribution remains suggestive rather than demonstrated.

The sample- and token-level selection deliberately reuse the same threshold τ_p to avoid an extra hyperparameter, but this couples the two decisions; it is unclear whether the token-level gains are truly attributable to token selection or partly an artifact of the induced effective sample subset at that threshold.

strengths: Introduces a clear, well-motivated and interpretable metric (Visual Information Gain) that quantifies visual dependency at both sample and token levels, enabling a genuinely data-centric approach to a well-known problem (language bias / visual ignorance in LVLMs).

Empirical validation is broad and consistent: improvements are demonstrated on four different LVLMs (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, ShareGPT4V 7B, Open-Qwen2VL 2B) across vision-understanding and hallucination benchmarks while using 34-79% of the original tokens, which is a meaningful data-efficiency result.

The supporting analyses are thorough and go beyond headline numbers: attention-fraction analysis (Fig. 5), text-corruption robustness (Fig. 6, Tab. E.1), preservation of text-only ability (Tab. 5), long-tail/task-composition analysis (Fig. E.3), and ablations over selection level (Tab. 6) and ratio (Fig. 7).
The paper shows orthogonality/complementarity with existing methods (VCD, PAI, VAR, LACING), which is a useful practical property and strengthens the contribution's relevance.

Reproducibility is reasonably addressed: thresholds, training configurations, compute budget, and the one-time forward-only nature of VIG scoring are documented in the appendix; the limitations (extra forward passes, limited model families) are discussed honestly.
weaknesses: There are apparent data-integrity/consistency problems. The text-only results for LLaVA-1.5 13B in Tab. E.2 (GSM8K 15.33, MMLU 51.68, HellaSwag 76.09, TruthfulQA 45.86) are identical to the 7B numbers in Tab. 5, which is almost certainly a copy error and undermines confidence in the reported numbers.

The ablation in Tab. 6 / Tab. F.1 reveals an unexplained anomaly: sample-level selection alone (SS) drops MMBench from 65.46 to 57.56, yet adding token-level selection (SS+TS) jumps it back to 66.33. A ~9-point swing attributable to token masking alone is not explained and raises questions about what is actually driving the gains.

The method is strongly hyperparameter-sensitive. In the ratio ablation (Tab. F.3), MMBench collapses to 56.87/56.44 at p=30/50 and only recovers at p=70. The reported headline results thus depend on a favorable choice of p, and the paper does not show how p would be selected without benchmark tuning.

The 'without image' condition is approximated by a Gaussian-blurred image rather than true image absence (Sec. 3.2, Appendix C). The model still receives visual tokens, so VIG conflates genuine visual grounding with the model's response to degraded visual input; this weakens the interpretation of the metric.

The benchmark-level alignment claim (Fig. 2) is purely qualitative (boxplots); no quantitative correlation between VIG and known modality dependency is provided. Moreover, negative VIG (e.g., GQA/SQA) is interpreted as 'text-dominance' when it may simply reflect the model being confused by the image, which is not distinguished.

The theoretical framing (Eqs. 4-5) assumes a Dirac/one-hot target so the entropy terms vanish, making the derivation somewhat circular; it does not provide a strong independent justification that VIG isolates visual grounding rather than answer difficulty/surprise.

Novelty is moderate: the core construction (comparing predictions with and without the image) closely resembles contrastive-decoding style measurements; the contribution is mainly the repurposing of this signal for data/token selection rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Presentation issues: the appendix contains a visibly corrupted table (repeated 'LW' rows and nonsensical text), and several tables have inconsistent/careless entries, suggesting insufficient proofreading.

strengths: Introduces Visual Information Gain (VIG), a simple and interpretable metric that quantifies the reduction in prediction uncertainty attributable to visual input at both sample and token levels.

Demonstrates data efficiency across four LVLMs: VIG-guided training reduces active tokens by 34% for LLaVA-1.5 7B, 79% for LLaVA-1.5 13B, 35% for ShareGPT4V 7B, and 41% for Open-Qwen2VL 2B while often improving benchmark performance (Table 3).
Provides token-level analyses showing VIG highlights visually grounded tokens such as colors, spatial relations, and attributes, and aligns with part-of-speech categories (Figures 3 and 4, Table 2).
Shows complementarity with existing visual grounding methods: combining VIG training with VCD, PAI, VAR, or LACING yields additive gains on several benchmarks (Table 4).

Includes text-only evaluations to check that visual grounding improvements do not degrade language capabilities (Table 5) and provides some qualitative examples of reduced hallucination (Appendix D.3).
Discusses some limitations, such as the computational overhead of VIG scoring and the limited architectural scope of the empirical study.
weaknesses: VIG is computed by comparing an original image against a blurred image, not by removing visual input entirely. This measures image clarity gain rather than visual information gain: the model still receives visual tokens, and a blurred image may retain low-level cues and introduce out-of-distribution effects. No validation against a true no-image condition is provided, undermining the central metric.

VIG is model-dependent and potentially circular. It is computed using a pretrained model that may already suffer from language bias. Filtering out low-VIG samples may discard exactly the text-dominant examples where the model needs to learn to use visual evidence, thereby reinforcing rather than mitigating bias. The claim of a 'model-agnostic' measure is therefore inaccurate.

Missing critical baselines. There is no comparison to random token selection at matched sparsity, nor to selecting tokens by high loss, entropy, or other criteria. The improvement from SS to SS+TS (Table 6) cannot be attributed specifically to VIG rather than to generic token masking or loss reweighting.

Confounded data distribution shift. VIG filtering heavily retains OCR-VQA (98.4%) and TextVQA (92.6%) while filtering GQA (44.2%) (Section 4.4, Figure E.3). Improvements on the chosen benchmarks may stem from this task-composition change rather than from VIG per se. Crucially, the paper does not evaluate on GQA, SQA, or VQAv2, so it cannot rule out degradation on the text-dominant multimodal tasks that were filtered out.

Experimental results contain suspicious inconsistencies and lack statistical rigor. In Table E.2, LLaVA-1.5 13B text-only results are exactly identical to LLaVA-1.5 7B in Table 5 across all four benchmarks, which is implausible. All experiments appear to be single runs with no seeds, error bars, or significance tests, despite many reported gains being within noise (e.g., POPE F1 +0.03, DocVQA +0.20, MMHal score +0.07).

Token-level selection reuses the sample-level threshold tau_p despite the two quantities having different distributions and scales. The resulting active-token fractions vary widely across models (about 42% to 79%), making the selection rule arbitrary and unprincipled. The paper provides no justification beyond avoiding an extra hyperparameter.

The random 70% baseline in Table 6 drops MMBench from 65.46 to 55.97, an unusually large degradation that suggests the baseline may be undertrained or the comparison may be unfair. This weakens the data-efficiency claim because the random subset should not lose 10 points if the training setup were properly controlled.

Several claims are overstated. The paper repeatedly says VIG is 'model-agnostic', that VIG training 'strictly improves over the vanilla baseline on all vision-understanding tasks', and that VIG 'aligns with benchmark-level modality dependency' without reporting a quantitative correlation. These overclaims are not adequately supported by the evidence.

Presentation and reproducibility issues. Appendix Table 1 is corrupted and unreadable. Several citation years are mismatched (e.g., Gao et al. 2023/2024, Goyal et al. 2023/2017, Gunjal et al. 2017/2024). The blur kernel hyperparameters are not specified, no code or VIG scores are released, and key evaluation details (e.g., how VIG is computed for Open-Qwen2VL) are missing.

The limitations discussion omits the most important risks: the blur approximation, the model-dependence and circularity of VIG, the heavy filtering of text-dominant multimodal data, and the resulting task-distribution confound.

strengths: Introduces Visual Information Gain (VIG), a simple and decomposable perplexity-based metric that quantifies the reduction in prediction uncertainty attributable to visual input at both sample and token levels.

Provides a clear theoretical derivation linking VIG to cross-entropy loss reduction and KL divergence, and empirically validates the metric against benchmark-level modality dependencies (e.g., COCO vs. GQA/SQA) and token-level grounding (e.g., colors, spatial relations, attributes).

Demonstrates strong data efficiency: on LLaVA-1.5 13B, VIG-guided selective training improves performance on all reported benchmarks while using only 12.14M active tokens vs. 58.61M for the vanilla model (79% reduction). Similar gains are shown for LLaVA-1.5 7B, ShareGPT4V 7B, and Open-Qwen2VL 2B.

Includes useful analyses showing that VIG-trained models allocate more attention to visual tokens, are more robust to textual corruption, and preserve text-only performance on GSM8K, MMLU, HellaSwag, and TruthfulQA.
Shows orthogonality with existing methods: combining VIG training with VCD, PAI, VAR, or LACING yields additive improvements, indicating that VIG is a complementary data-centric strategy.
Provides an honest limitations discussion (e.g., VIG computation overhead, scope limited to LLaVA/ShareGPT families) and an ethics/impact statement.
Thorough appendix with additional qualitative examples, benchmark details, thresholds, hyperparameters, and data distribution analysis.
weaknesses: The 'without visual information' condition is simulated with a blurred image rather than a true image-absent condition. Blurred images may still leak low-level cues (e.g., color, layout), so VIG may underestimate the true visual gain and its ranking could be affected.

The token-level selection claim is not fully isolated: there is no control experiment comparing VIG-guided token selection against random token masking at the same sparsity. It is therefore unclear whether the gains from token-level VIG filtering exceed generic token sparsification.

The same threshold tau_p is reused for both sample-level and token-level selection without justification. Since sample-level VIG is an average of token-level VIG, this choice may be suboptimal and introduces an implicit coupling that is not ablated.

Results are reported from a single training run without error bars or multiple seeds. Given the use of GPT-based evaluation and stochastic fine-tuning, the magnitude of some improvements may be within noise.

Presentation issues reduce clarity: several citations appear mismatched (e.g., ShareGPT4V vs. MiniGPT-v2 reference labels) and the appendix contains a corrupted table ('Table 1: The performance of the LW and LW models on the 100000...').

The claim of 'superior performance' is not uniformly supported: VIG alone is competitive but not strictly best on all metrics (e.g., LACING achieves better MMVet and CHAIR scores), though the combination with LACING is stronger.

The total computational overhead of VIG scoring (two forward passes per sample) and its trade-off against the achieved token savings is not quantified in detail, making it difficult to assess the overall cost-effectiveness.
